opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and honestly it's a bit counterintuitive. People often assume the bottleneck in robotics is perception: more cameras, better tactile sensors, depth, force-torque, all of that. And those things can help. But when we look at where our policies actually fail, a surprising number of failures aren't because the robot can't see something right now. They happen because the robot doesn't remember what it saw or did a few seconds or a few minutes ago.

Take something like cleaning up a kitchen or folding a basket of laundry. Partway through, the robot needs to know which drawers it already checked, whether it already wiped that counter, or which step of a multi-stage task it's on. If the policy only conditions on the current observation, it can get stuck in loops: it opens a cabinet, closes it, opens it again. Adding a wrist camera or a tactile sensor doesn't solve that. The information just isn't in the current frame anymore. It's in the history.

Hardware choices also compound. Every new sensor has to go on every robot, be calibrated, be robust, and then you need data collected with that sensor. That fragments your data and makes it harder to train one general model across many platforms. Memory is a modeling choice. You can improve it with the same cameras and the same data you already have, and the gains transfer across embodiments.

That said, memory isn't trivial to add. Naively feeding in long histories of images is expensive, and policies can latch onto spurious correlations in the past, like copying the previous action instead of reacting to what's happening. So a lot of the work is figuring out the right representation: what to remember, at what granularity, maybe compressing it into something closer to language or a compact latent rather than raw pixels.

So it's not that sensors don't matter. It's that for the long-horizon, real-world tasks we care about, the missing ingredient has more often been context over time than richer input at a single moment.

r001.rationale: The response says many policy failures come from not remembering past observations or actions, rather than from insufficient sensing, and explains that more sensors would not solve those failures.

r002.rationale: It describes policies that condition only on the current observation, but does not state that most of Chelsea Finn’s team’s current policies lack memory of previous observations.

r003.rationale: It says memory can improve performance using existing cameras and data, but does not claim that commercially viable robots are possible for some applications without adding sensors.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, it's a good question, and I think the honest answer is that most of the failures we see in the real world aren't perception failures in the sense of the robot not having enough information in the moment. They're failures of the robot not knowing what it already did, or what it already saw a few seconds ago.

So a concrete example. You ask a robot to put the dishes away, and it opens a cabinet, puts a plate in, closes the cabinet, turns back to the counter. Now it picks up the next plate, and it has no idea it just closed that cabinet. It'll sometimes go try to put the plate through a closed door, or reopen it, or wander. More sensors don't help you there. You could put another camera on it and it would still make the same mistake, because the information it needs isn't in the current frame. It's in the history.

And I think there's something a little seductive about sensors because they're easy to reason about. If the robot can't see behind the object, add a wrist camera. If it can't feel the contact, add tactile. Those are real and they matter for some tasks. But for a lot of the long-horizon stuff that we actually care about, the thing that's missing is this ability to carry context forward. Where did I put that? Has this person asked me to do this already? Did I already check the top shelf?

The other reason is more practical. Every sensor you add is something you have to collect data for, something that can break, something that changes the distribution of inputs so your model trained on one platform doesn't transfer to another. Memory is kind of the opposite. If you can get the model to use its own history well, you're extracting more out of the data and the hardware you already have, instead of making the hardware more complicated.

And there's a nice parallel with language models here. A lot of what made them feel capable wasn't that they got more input modalities. It was that they could condition on a long context and actually use it. I think robotics is behind on that, mostly because it's genuinely harder. The training data is shorter, the horizons are long, and it's very easy for a model to just learn to ignore its history and act reactively because that gets you most of the way on short tasks. So you have to be pretty deliberate about it.

So I wouldn't say sensors don't matter. I'd say that if I have to pick where the next big jump in capability comes from, I think it comes from robots that remember, not robots that see slightly better.

r001.rationale: The response says many robot failures stem from not using past actions or observations, and that adding sensors would not fix those failures. It presents memory as the more important capability bottleneck.

r002.rationale: It describes many real-world failures as robots forgetting what they did or saw, but does not state that most of Chelsea Finn’s team’s current robot policies lack memory of previous observations.

r003.rationale: The response argues that memory can improve capability without complicating hardware, but it does not assert that commercially viable robots can serve some applications without added sensors.

astra-6.text:
I think the key distinction is between what the robot can observe right now and what it needs to know to accomplish a task. More sensors can give you a richer picture of the current moment, but that doesn’t necessarily tell you what happened earlier.

If you’re looking for an object and you’ve already checked a drawer, you want the robot to remember that it checked the drawer and the object wasn’t there. If it’s putting things away, it needs to keep track of what it’s already done. You can’t necessarily recover that information by adding another camera.

So I wouldn’t say more sensors aren’t useful. But for longer tasks, memory lets the robot use the information it’s already collected, instead of treating every moment as a new problem. That seems like a pretty fundamental capability to build.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts current sensing with information about earlier events, but does not say sensing is not the main bottleneck in robot development.

r002.rationale: It argues that robots need memory for longer tasks, but does not state that most of Finn’s team’s current policies lack memory of previous observations.

r003.rationale: It does not claim commercially viable robots are possible for any applications without adding sensors.

sol-6.1.text:
I think more sensors can be useful, but there are a lot of things you can’t infer from what you’re sensing at a single instant. If a robot puts something in a drawer and then closes the drawer, another camera isn’t necessarily going to tell it where that object is. It needs to remember what happened before.

And that applies to interaction, too. If you try to pick something up and it slips, that tells you something about the object and how you should grasp it next time. You want the robot to use that experience rather than treating every attempt as a completely new problem. So I’d prioritize memory because it lets the robot make better use of the sensors it already has, across time.

r001.rationale: The response favors memory because single-moment sensing can miss information, but it does not say sensing is not the main bottleneck in robot development.

r002.rationale: It says robots need to remember prior events, but does not state that most of Finn’s team’s current robot policies lack memory of previous observations.
